From pipeline to power: what will determine which data centre projects get built?
The data centre pipeline is booming, but proposed capacity does not automatically translate into electricity demand. Understanding which projects are credible, and which can realistically secure power, is becoming essential for large-load consumers and utilities alike

The data centre boom is reshaping electricity demand. AI adoption, cloud computing and increasingly power-intensive digital infrastructure are driving rapid growth in proposed capacity, creating new opportunities and challenges for both large-load consumers and the utilities expected to serve them. 
But headline pipeline numbers only tell part of the story. 
Wood Mackenzie is tracking 434 GW of planned data centre capacity in the US, while 78 GW is currently under construction. The gap highlights an increasingly important question: which projects are most likely to materialise, and how will they secure the power they need? 
Which projects are most likely to materialise? 
Not every gigawatt in the development pipeline carries the same level of certainty. 
A newly announced development is fundamentally different from one progressing through permitting, securing customers and capital, or moving towards construction. Utility engagement provides another important signal as projects move from initial requests towards firmer commitments for electricity supply. 
For utilities facing a growing queue of large-load requests, understanding these differences is essential for determining when and where demand is likely to emerge. 
For large-load consumers and developers, the challenge is the other side of the same equation: demonstrating that projects are credible while establishing a viable route to power. 
Can projects secure enough power, quickly enough? 
Even commercially credible projects face another hurdle: whether sufficient power can be delivered on the timeline required. 
Data centres can move from concept towards development more quickly than new generation, transmission and other energy infrastructure can always be built. In constrained power markets, that mismatch can become a significant obstacle to project development. 
In PJM, for example, Wood Mackenzie’s view of accredited risked supply is around 80 GW below high-confidence large-load demand. 
For utilities, this creates difficult decisions around forecasting demand and planning generation and infrastructure investment. For data centre developers and other large-load consumers, it makes understanding local grid conditions and future power availability increasingly important to development strategy. 
Commercially credible demand, in other words, is not necessarily deliverable demand. 
What happens when the grid cannot meet the timeline? 
Grid constraints do not necessarily mean projects disappear. Instead, they can change how projects secure their power. 
Large data centre developments are already exploring a broader range of supply arrangements as they seek to reconcile rapid development schedules with slower-moving energy infrastructure. Wood Mackenzie is tracking more than 100 disclosed US data centre sites with around-the-meter generation configurations, which includes behind-the-meter onsite power as well as front-of-the-meter generation onsite or at nearby nodes. 
These approaches add another layer to the demand picture. Large-load consumers need to assess which combination of grid supply and alternative power options can support their development plans. Utilities need visibility into how those choices could affect the timing, location and characteristics of future electricity demand. 
Moving from potential demand to deliverable demand 
The scale of data centre growth is significant, but understanding its impact on the power sector requires more than counting announced gigawatts. 
Utilities need to understand which loads are likely to materialise and when. Large-load consumers need to understand where power can realistically be secured, on what timeline and through which supply options. 
Increasingly, these are two sides of the same challenge. 
Distinguishing between potential demand, credible demand and demand that the energy system can realistically serve will be essential for both sides as the market develops. 
Not all gigawatts are equal. The next phase of data centre growth will be shaped not simply by how much capacity is proposed, but by which projects can successfully make the journey from pipeline to power.
